bib.title: From Crowdsourced Data to High-Quality Benchmarks: Arena-Hard and BenchBuilder Pipeline
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv v2, 14 Oct 2024; ICML 2025 per caller, not printed in text)

question: Can an LLM pipeline curate challenging open-ended prompts from crowdsourced data into a benchmark that separates models with confidence and agrees with human preference rankings, cheaply and automatically?
hypothesis: Prompts scoring high on seven quality criteria and sampled evenly across topic clusters yield a benchmark with higher separability and human-alignment than random or hand-written prompt sets.
contributions: BenchBuilder: automated pipeline curating high-quality benchmarks from crowdsourced data

Metrics for separability and human alignment (Separability with Confidence, Agreement with Confidence, Pair Rank Brier Score); Arena-Hard-Auto shows higher separation and alignment than existing benchmarks

method.summary: Embed 200K Chatbot Arena prompts, cluster into 4,000 topics, score each prompt 0-7 on seven criteria with GPT-4-Turbo, keep prompts >=6 in clusters with mean >=5, sample 2 prompts from each of 250 clusters to get 500 prompts. Models are judged pairwise against GPT-4-0314 by GPT-4-Turbo with own-answer chain of thought, two position-swapped games, Bradley-Terry scores and bootstrap CIs.
method.task: benchmark curation and LLM-as-a-judge pairwise evaluation of chat models

datasets.name: Chatbot Arena prompts
datasets.size: 200,000 prompts initial pool; 4,000 clusters; >500 high-quality clusters; 500 final prompts (75K Chatbot Arena queries used for random baselines and Table 11)
datasets.preprocessing: Remove duplicates, multi-turn, non-English; remove PII and offensive content

datasets.name: WildChat-1M
datasets.size: 150,000 queries; 185 high-quality clusters with 4,500+ prompts; Wild-Hard-Auto = 250 prompts (2 from each of top 125 clusters)

other.note: pairwise comparison baseline, win rate 50.0 in Table 13
alternative judges in Table 4; Llama-3-70B also alt annotator

models.name: Top-20 Chatbot Arena models (2024/04/13) and 50+ leaderboard models

other.use: prompt embeddings, then UMAP and HDBSCAN (BERTopic)

inference.samples: 2 games per query (positions swapped) = 1000 judgments per model; 100 bootstrap rounds for 95% CI
inference.prompting: Judge generates its own answer first (chain of thought) then verdict on 5-point Likert [[A>>B]] to [[B>>A]]; quality annotator explains each of 7 criteria then lists satisfied criteria

parameters.style_features: answer token length, markdown header, bold, list density; normalised (A-B)/(A+B)
parameters.scoring: Bradley-Terry vs baseline; style-controlled variant adds style coefficients

metrics.name: Separability with Confidence
metrics.definition: Percentage of model pairs with non-overlapping bootstrap confidence intervals of benchmark scores

metrics.name: Agreement with Confidence Interval
metrics.definition: Per model pair: +1 if both benchmarks confidently separate and agree, -1 if disagree, 0 if either cannot separate; averaged over pairs

metrics.name: Pair Rank Brier Score
metrics.definition: Mean over model pairs of (bootstrap-predicted P(model i < model j) - ground-truth outcome)^2, normal approximation of bootstrap distribution

metrics.name: Spearman and Kendall Tau
metrics.definition: Rank correlation of benchmark ranking with Chatbot Arena ranking

eval.protocol: Reference = Chatbot Arena English ranking (2024/04/13) or its English Hard Prompts / style-controlled version; top-20 models also on AlpacaEval; 95% CI via 100 bootstrap rounds; no human raters in the loop; MT-Bench and AlpacaEval results from their recommended setups / repository

prompts.text: Your task is to evaluate how well the following input prompts can assess the capabilities of advanced AI assistants. For the input prompt, please analyze it based on the following 7 criteria. For each criteria, make sure to explain before determine whether the input satisfy it. 1. Specificity ... 7. Real-World Application ... you must list the criteria numbers that the prompt satisfies in the format of a Python array. For example, "Criteria Satisfied: [1, 2, 4, 6, 7]".

Please act as an impartial judge and evaluate the quality of the responses provided by two AI assistants to the user prompt displayed below. ... Begin your evaluation by generating your own answer to the prompt. You must provide your answers before judging any answers. ... [[A>>B]] [[A>B]] [[A=B]] [[B>A]] [[B>>A]]

detailed: "You are a helpful assistant who thoroughly explains things with as much detail as possible."; chatty: "You are a helpful assistant who is chatty."; md: "You are a helpful assistant who uses as much markdown as possible."; no-md: "You are a helpful assistant who never uses markdown."

evidence.quote: we obtain 95% confidence intervals of model performances via applying 100 rounds of bootstrapping

results.claim: Arena-Hard-Auto has 3x higher separation than MT-Bench and 98.6% correlation with human preference rankings at $20 (abstract headline).
results.setup: Abstract; headline 98.6% is the style-controlled agreement vs Chatbot Arena English Hard Prompts (Table 3), not the Table 1 Spearman
results.note: Abstract calls it 'correlation'; Table 3 shows it is Confidence Agreement (and Spearman) with style control against the Hard Prompts (English) leaderboard. Without style control Table 1 gives Spearman 93.2%.
results.quote: achieves 98.6% correlation with human preference rankings, all at a cost of $20

results.claim: Arena-Hard-Auto separability vs MT-Bench and AlpacaEval 2.0 LC.
results.setup: Top-20 Chatbot Arena models (2024/04/13) also on AlpacaEval leaderboard; reference = Chatbot Arena English ranking; GPT-4-Turbo judge; baseline gpt-4-0314; 95% CI from 100 bootstrap rounds
results.note: Table 1: MT-Bench 22.6%, AlpacaEval 2.0 LC 83.2%, Chatbot Arena 85.8%
results.quote: Arena-Hard-Auto shows the highest separability (87.4%) against widely adopted LLM benchmarks

results.claim: Arena-Hard-Auto confidence agreement with Chatbot Arena (English) in Table 1; MT-Bench 26.6, AlpacaEval LC 82.5.
results.setup: Top-20 Chatbot Arena models (2024/04/13) also on AlpacaEval leaderboard; reference = Chatbot Arena English ranking; GPT-4-Turbo judge; baseline gpt-4-0314; 95% CI from 100 bootstrap rounds
results.note: Text of Sec 6.2 prints 90.8% for the same quantity; Table 1 prints 90.9%.
results.table: Table 1, row Confidence Agreement, column Arena-Hard-Auto (MT-Bench 26.6%, AlpacaEval 2.0 LC 82.5%)

results.claim: MT-Bench has high Spearman (89.9%) but low confidence agreement, showing Spearman hides ranking variance.
results.setup: Top-20 Chatbot Arena models (2024/04/13) also on AlpacaEval leaderboard; reference = Chatbot Arena English ranking; GPT-4-Turbo judge; baseline gpt-4-0314; 95% CI from 100 bootstrap rounds
results.note: Text says confidence agreement 22.6%, but Table 1 prints 22.6% as MT-Bench Separability and 26.6% as MT-Bench Confidence Agreement. Table 3 prints 30.3% / 22.6% / 90.7% for MT-Bench with a different reference.
results.quote: we observe a significant gap between MT-bench’s Spearman Correlation (89.9%) and confidence agreement (22.6%) to Chatbot Arena

results.claim: Brier score of Arena-Hard-Auto (lower is better) vs MT-Bench and AlpacaEval LC.
results.setup: Top-20 Chatbot Arena models (2024/04/13) also on AlpacaEval leaderboard; reference = Chatbot Arena English ranking; GPT-4-Turbo judge; baseline gpt-4-0314; 95% CI from 100 bootstrap rounds
results.table: Table 1, row Brier Score, column Arena-Hard-Auto (MT-Bench 0.09, AlpacaEval 2.0 LC 0.11)

results.claim: Against the Chatbot Arena English Hard Prompts leaderboard with style control on both sides, Arena-Hard-Auto reaches 98.6% confidence agreement.
results.setup: Style-controlled GPT-4-Turbo judge vs style-controlled Chatbot Arena battles (English Hard Prompts), top-20 models
results.quote: style controlled Arena-Hard-Auto achieves 98.6% agreement and correlation to style controlled human preference ranking
results.table: Table 3, row Confidence Agreement, column Arena-Hard-Auto (Style Control) (98.6%; Arena-Hard-Auto 94.4%, AlpacaEval LC 83.8%, MT-Bench 30.3%)

results.claim: Style-controlled Arena-Hard-Auto separability is 86.8% versus 87.4% without control.
results.setup: Table 3 setup
results.table: Table 3, row Separability, column Arena-Hard-Auto (Style Control)

results.claim: Against Chatbot Arena Hard Prompts (English), unmodified Arena-Hard-Auto gets 98.6% confidence agreement and Brier 0.055.
results.setup: Arena-Hard-Auto, gpt-4-1106-preview judge, vs Chatbot Arena Category Hard Prompt (English), top-20 models
results.note: Sec 6.3 says 98.6% Confidence Agreement and 96.7% Spearman; Table 3 prints Spearman 94.9% for unmodified Arena-Hard-Auto with its own reference.
results.table: Table 9, row Confiderence Agreement (Spearman 96.7%, Kendall 87.4%, Brier 0.055)

results.claim: Judge choice matters: GPT-4-Turbo confidence agreement 90.9% vs Claude-3-Opus 66.7%, Gemini-1.5-Pro 84.8%, Llama-3-70B 65.6%.
results.setup: Arena-Hard-Auto ranking vs Chatbot Arena English (2024/04/13), judge swapped
results.table: Table 4, row Confiderence Agreement, column Claude3-Opus (GPT4-T 90.9, Gemini1.5-Pro 84.8, Llama3-70B 65.6, Ensemble 91.5)

results.claim: Ensemble of GPT-4-Turbo and Gemini-1.5-Pro as judges raises separability to 89.5% and Spearman to 96.5%.

results.table: Table 4, row Separability, column Ensemble-as-Judges (Spearman 96.5, Brier 0.065)

results.claim: Self-bias check: GPT-4-Turbo judge ranks OpenAI models 0.6 places above human ranking and Claude models 0.8 below; ensemble gives -0.4 and +0.4.
results.setup: Ranking shift vs Chatbot Arena Hard Prompts leaderboard; 5 GPT and 4 Claude models
results.table: Table 10, row column average, OpenAI GPT Series, column GPT-4-turbo (0.6; Claude -0.8; Ensemble -0.4 and 0.4)

results.claim: BenchBuilder on WildChat: Wild-Hard-Auto beats a 250-prompt random WildChat sample on confidence agreement (88.6% vs 36.4%).
results.setup: GPT-4-Turbo judge; 150,000 WildChat queries; 125 clusters x 2 prompts = 250 prompts
results.table: Table 2, row Confidence Agreement, column Wild-Hard-Auto (Wild-Random-250 36.4%; separability 86.7% vs 75.6%; Spearman 91.5% vs 45.5%)

results.claim: Arena-Hard-Auto beats two random 500-prompt Chatbot Arena samples: confidence agreement 84.2% vs 57.5% and 66.1%.
results.setup: Random samples of 500 prompts from 75K Chatbot Arena queries; top-20 models; each prompt judged once with baseline answer first
results.note: Values differ from Table 1 (90.9/87.4/93.2) because Table 7 judges each prompt once, not twice with swapped positions.
results.table: Table 7, row Confiderence Agreement (separability 80.5 vs 74.7 and 76.3; Spearman 94.7 vs 64.7 and 72.5; Brier 0.069 vs 0.215 and 0.162)

results.claim: Llama-3-70B-Instruct as the prompt annotator gives similar gains: Llama-Hard-Auto confidence agreement 86.0% vs random 55.8% and 58.1%.

results.table: Table 8, row Confidence Agreement, column Llama-Hard-Auto (Arena-Hard-Auto-500 88.4%)

results.claim: Quality score tracks separability: win-rate between model pairs becomes more separable as the BenchBuilder quality score rises.
results.setup: 50 queries per quality score 0-7, bootstrapped win-rate and CI on score intervals of 2; GPT-4-0613 vs Llama-2-70b-chat, Claude-3-Sonnet vs Haiku, Mistral-Large vs Mixtral; GPT-4-Turbo judge
results.quote: We observe a similar trend of win-rate between model pairs becomes increasingly separable as the quality score increases.

limits: Seven qualities may skew toward technical domains.
Single-judge self-bias exists (GPT-4-Turbo ranks GPT models slightly above human ranking, Claude below); ensemble is only a first step.
Agreement is measured on 20 models against one Chatbot Arena snapshot (2024/04/13); small number of model pairs.
Models and judges (gpt-4-1106-preview) are dated; cost figures use 2024 pricing.
